content: Pain in the pharynx is the most common symptom of a sore throat. In children, sore throat can be categorized as acute, subacute, or recurrent. The most frequent causes include bacterial, viral, and protozoal organisms. While sore throat is often self-limiting, it can sometimes be associated with more severe forms of disease. Treatment is generally conservative, but antibiotics or antivirals may be prescribed depending on the underlying cause and the severity of the clinical presentation. Historically, sore throat has been recognized and studied for centuries. In 1879, R.L. described various forms of sore throat in the British Medical Journal. By 1910, Dr. Donelan emphasized the importance of laboratory testing in diagnosis. In 1931, W.M.W. noted that infections such as whooping cough and measles were linked to chronic nasopharyngitis. Sore throat can be classified into infectious and non-infectious causes. Infectious causes include: Bacterial: Group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Treponema pallidum, and Fusobacterium. Viral: Adenovirus, Coxsackievirus, Enterovirus, Influenza, Parainfluenza, Epstein-Barr virus, Coronaviruses, Poliovirus, and Rhinovirus. Protozoal: Babesia microti and Toxoplasma gondii (less common). Fungal: Candida species. Non-infectious causes include: Autoimmune conditions: Steven-Johnson syndrome, Behçet’s disease, Kawasaki disease, and PFAPA syndrome. Trauma: Insertion of sharp objects into the throat. Chemical exposure: Smoking and air pollutants. Physical factors: Snoring, shouting, or tracheal intubation. The pathophysiology of sore throat involves the activation of sensory nerves in the pharynx by prostaglandins and bradykinin, leading to pain. Fever results from cytokine release, which enhances the host’s immune response to infection but may also cause headache. Cranial nerves supplying the nasopharynx mediate pain perception. Bradykinin-induced vasodilation in the nasal epithelium contributes to nasal congestion. Inflammation in the nasopharynx stimulates the trigeminal nerves, causing sneezing. When inflammation reaches the larynx, sensory nerve stimulation triggers coughing. Inflammatory mediators acting on airway sensory nerve endings can lead to heightened cough reflex sensitivity. In children, sore throat can arise from common causes or be acutely life-threatening. Bacterial causes: Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (most common), Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Viral causes: Rhinovirus, Coronavirus, Respiratory Syncytial Virus, Metapneumovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus. Life-threatening causes: Epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess, parapharyngeal abscess, peritonsillar abscess, diphtheria, and infectious mononucleosis. Other causes: Trauma, psychogenic factors, and autoimmune conditions. Differentiating sore throat from other diseases requires a detailed clinical history and physical examination. Sore throat is a symptom that can present in various diseases, often as an initial complaint. Epidemiologically, sore throat is one of the most common medical conditions, primarily caused by viruses and bacteria. Group A Streptococcus (GAS) is the most common bacterial cause, responsible for 15-25% of pharyngitis cases in children and 10% in adults. Diagnosing GAS is crucial for treatment and reducing infectivity, as well as preventing post-infectious complications. Acute suppurative complications include retropharyngeal and peritonsillar abscesses, acute bacterial sinusitis, cervical adenitis, and acute otitis media. Late non-suppurative complications include acute rheumatic fever (ARF) and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. In adults, non-suppurative complications do not require immediate treatment. Risk factors for sore throat include lack of vaccination, weakened immunity, frequent or chronic sinus infections, age, allergies, exposure to chemical irritants or tobacco smoke, and close living spaces. The natural history of sore throat typically involves a course of respiratory tract or oropharyngeal infections, with an asymptomatic incubation period of 1-4 days. Early symptoms include throat pain, itching, and discomfort, while severe cases may involve difficulty swallowing or breathing. Fever, myalgias, arthralgias, rhinorrhea, and cough may accompany the infection, depending on its type. Untreated infectious conditions can lead to complications such as sinusitis, mastoiditis, otitis media, cervical lymphadenitis, retropharyngeal abscess, parapharyngeal abscess, quinsy, and sepsis. Non-suppurative complications include acute glomerulonephritis, acute rheumatic fever, and reactive arthritis. Prognosis is generally excellent, with most patients recovering spontaneously within 7-10 days. Early identification and treatment minimize complications. Symptoms of sore throat include sudden onset of throat pain and fever. Other symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, headache, malaise, difficulty swallowing, and abdominal pain. Viral causes often present with cough, conjunctivitis, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea. Physical findings may include redness and swelling of the tonsils and pharynx, tender and enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes, and pharyngeal exudate that can be easily scraped off. Physical examination findings vary depending on the etiology. Notable findings include: Exudative pharyngitis, petechiae on the posterior palate, and anterior cervical lymphadenopathy in streptococcal pharyngitis. Thick white exudate with a membranous covering of the tonsils that cannot be removed without bleeding in diphtheria. Erythematous pharynx with posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly in infectious mononucleosis. Vesicular rash on the posterior pharynx in herpangina and on the hands, feet, and mouth in hand-foot-mouth disease (both caused by Coxsackievirus). Diffuse erythematous rash in scarlet fever. Stridor, respiratory distress, dysphagia, and odynophagia with high-grade fever in life-threatening conditions such as quinsy, retropharyngeal abscess, parapharyngeal abscess, epiglottitis, and laryngotracheobronchitis. Significant tonsillar asymmetry, suggesting peritonsillar abscess. Vesicles on the buccal mucosa, raising suspicion for herpetic gingivostomatitis. Strawberry tongue, generalized oropharyngeal erythema, cracked red lips, cervical lymphadenopathy, non-purulent conjunctivitis, and desquamation of the periunugal region in Kawasaki disease. Laboratory findings help narrow down the diagnosis. Rapid Antigen Detection Test (RADT) is the first-line diagnostic test for GAS pharyngitis. A positive test confirms GAS infection, warranting antibiotic treatment. A negative test requires follow-up throat culture. Throat culture is highly sensitive (90-99%) and used in non-emergency situations or when RADT is negative. Antistreptococcal antibodies confirm previous GAS infection in cases of acute rheumatic fever or other non-suppurative complications. Monospot test diagnoses infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. Peripheral blood smear shows atypical lymphocytes in infectious mononucleosis. CBC, ESR, and CRP have low predictive value and are not routinely used. Imaging studies are reserved for complicated cases. Neck X-rays (lateral view) are used for suspected epiglottitis, showing the characteristic thumbprint sign. CT scans are not specific for sore throat but may help diagnose complications such as retropharyngeal abscess, peritonsillar abscess, and suppurative cervical lymphadenitis. Treatment for sore throat in most children involves supportive care and systemic analgesia. Acetaminophen, NSAIDs, and steam inhalation alleviate pain. Corticosteroids may be considered for pain unresponsive to simple analgesics. Antibiotics are not routinely needed but are reserved for high-risk children (e.g., immunosuppressed, history of rheumatic heart disease) to prevent complications. Penicillin is the antibiotic of choice, with alternatives including amoxicillin, erythromycin, azithromycin, or first-generation cephalosporins for those with penicillin hypersensitivity. Surgical interventions are indicated in specific cases. Complete tonsillectomy is recommended for recurrent tonsillitis (≥7 episodes/year, ≥5/year for 2 consecutive years, or ≥3/year for 3 consecutive years). Partial tonsillectomy is preferred for tonsillar hyperplasia with obstructive symptoms. Aspiration or tonsillectomy puncture is used to drain tonsillar abscesses. Preventive measures include regular handwashing, separating and thoroughly cleaning eating utensils of infected individuals, cleaning toys of infected toddlers, disposing of dirty tissues, and ensuring children with strep throat complete 24 hours of antibiotics before returning to school.
